claim: Deletion of Kip2 results in nuclear migration defects in budding yeast.
source: Deletion of this kinesin results in nuclear migration defects, and the phenotype is associated with shorter, less abundant cytoplasmic microtubules (Cottingham and Hoyt, 1997; Huyett et al., 1998; Miller et al., 1998; Caudron et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior published work

claim: Deletion of Kip2 is associated with shorter, less abundant cytoplasmic microtubules.
source: Deletion of this kinesin results in nuclear migration defects, and the phenotype is associated with shorter, less abundant cytoplasmic microtubules (Cottingham and Hoyt, 1997; Huyett et al., 1998; Miller et al., 1998; Caudron et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior published work

claim: Kip2 overexpression results in hyper-elongated cytoplasmic microtubules.
source: Conversely, Kip2 overexpression results in hyper-elongated cytoplasmic microtubules (Carvalho et al., 2004).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior published work

claim: The stabilization of microtubules by Kip2 is thought to be indirect and a consequence of Kip2 transporting Bik1 (Clip170) to microtubule plus ends.
source: The stabilization of microtubules by Kip2 is thought to be indirect and a consequence of Kip2 transporting the growth regulator Bik1 (Clip170) to microtubule plus ends (Carvalho et al., 2004; Caudron et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior published work

claim: Kip2 strongly increased the length of freshly polymerized microtubules within 10 minutes.
source: Within 10 min, Kip2 (Figure 1B,C), as well as Kip2-enhanced green fluorescent protein (eGFP) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A), strongly increased the length of freshly polymerized microtubules (p<0.0001, Welch's unpaired t-test, please refer to Table 1 for porcine microtubule parameter values).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in figures and statistical analysis

claim: Kip2-eGFP strongly increased the length of freshly polymerized microtubules within 10 minutes.
source: Within 10 min, Kip2 (Figure 1B,C), as well as Kip2-enhanced green fluorescent protein (eGFP) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A), strongly increased the length of freshly polymerized microtubules (p<0.0001, Welch's unpaired t-test, please refer to Table 1 for porcine microtubule parameter values).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in figures and statistical analysis

claim: The effect of Kip2 on microtubule length was almost completely inhibited when ATP was replaced by AMP-PNP.
source: The effect of Kip2 on microtubule length was almost completely inhibited when ATP was replaced by the non-hydrolyzable ATP analog adenylyl imidodiphosphate (AMP-PNP) (Figure 1C, blue markers, p<0.0001), showing that growth promotion requires ATP hydrolysis.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in figures and statistical analysis

claim: Growth promotion by Kip2 requires ATP hydrolysis.
source: The effect of Kip2 on microtubule length was almost completely inhibited when ATP was replaced by the non-hydrolyzable ATP analog adenylyl imidodiphosphate (AMP-PNP) (Figure 1C, blue markers, p<0.0001), showing that growth promotion requires ATP hydrolysis.
evidence: Inferred from the experimental result that AMP-PNP inhibits the effect

claim: Kip2 increased the growth rate of microtubules 2.9-fold.
source: Kip2 increased the growth rate of microtubules (the slope of the growing microtubule in the kymograph) 2.9-fold (Figure 1E).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in figures

claim: Kip2 reduced the frequency of catastrophe approximately 10-fold.
source: In addition, Kip2 reduced the frequency of catastrophe (the transition between growth and shrinkage phases) approximately 10-fold (Figure 1F).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in figures

claim: Kip2 did not affect the shrinkage rate of microtubules.
source: Kip2 did not affect the shrinkage rate (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B), or the frequency of rescue (the transition between shrinkage and growth phases, Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in figures

claim: Kip2 did not affect the frequency of rescue.
source: Kip2 did not affect the shrinkage rate (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B), or the frequency of rescue (the transition between shrinkage and growth phases, Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in figures

claim: The half-maximal stimulation of polymerization and inhibition of catastrophe occurred at approximately 7 nM Kip2.
source: The half-maximal stimulation of polymerization and inhibition of catastrophe occurred at ≈7 nM Kip2.
evidence: Supported by experimental data analysis

claim: The cellular concentration of Kip2 is approximately 25 nM.
source: Given that the cellular concentration of Kip2 is ≈25 nM (Ghaemmaghami et al., 2003), these results show that Kip2 affects microtubule dynamics in vitro at physiologically relevant concentrations.
evidence: Supported by citation to prior published work

claim: Kip2 affects microtubule dynamics in vitro at physiologically relevant concentrations.
source: Given that the cellular concentration of Kip2 is ≈25 nM (Ghaemmaghami et al., 2003), these results show that Kip2 affects microtubule dynamics in vitro at physiologically relevant concentrations.
evidence: Inferred from comparison of in vitro effective concentration with cellular concentration

claim: Kip2 increased the yeast microtubule growth rate by 2.3-fold.
source: Consistent with our porcine tubulin results, Kip2 increased the yeast microtubule growth rate by 2.3-fold and inhibited catastrophe 20-fold (Figure 1—figure supplement 2B,C).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in figures

claim: Kip2 inhibited catastrophe of yeast microtubules 20-fold.
source: Consistent with our porcine tubulin results, Kip2 increased the yeast microtubule growth rate by 2.3-fold and inhibited catastrophe 20-fold (Figure 1—figure supplement 2B,C).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in figures

claim: The half-maximal stimulation of polymerization and inhibition of catastrophe for yeast tubulin occurred at approximately 12 nM Kip2.
source: The half-maximal stimulation of polymerization and inhibition of catastrophe for yeast tubulin occurred at ≈12 nM Kip2, similar to the concentration at which Kip2 regulates porcine brain microtubules.
evidence: Supported by experimental data analysis

claim: Kip2 is a microtubule polymerase and anti-catastrophe factor in vitro.
source: In summary, Kip2 is a microtubule polymerase and anti-catastrophe factor in vitro and does not require additional proteins such as Bik1 for these activities.
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing increased growth rate and decreased catastrophe frequency

claim: Kip2 does not require additional proteins such as Bik1 for its polymerase and anti-catastrophe activities.
source: In summary, Kip2 is a microtubule polymerase and anti-catastrophe factor in vitro and does not require additional proteins such as Bik1 for these activities.
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing Kip2 alone is sufficient for these activities

claim: Kip2 doubled the effective tubulin association rate constant (kon) to 1.5 μM-1·s-1 from 0.7 μM-1·s-1 in the absence of Kip2.
source: By measuring the rate of growth of porcine microtubules from guanylyl (α,β)methylene-diphosphonate (GMPCPP) seeds over a range of tubulin concentrations (Figure 1—figure supplement 3A), we found that Kip2 doubled the effective tubulin association rate constant (kon, the rate that tubulin is stably incorporated into the microtubule lattice) to 1.5 μM-1.s-1 (at the plus end) from 0.7 μM-1.s-1 in the absence of Kip2.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in figures

claim: Kip2 facilitated microtubule nucleation on seeds, with robust growth observed at tubulin concentrations as low as 4 μM, compared with 10 μM in the absence of Kip2.
source: In addition to accelerating the net addition of subunits, Kip2 also facilitated microtubule nucleation on the seeds, with robust growth observed at tubulin concentrations as low as 4 μM, compared with 10 μM in the absence of Kip2 (Figure 1—figure supplement 3A).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in figures

claim: Kip2 acted like a nucleation factor in analogy to XMAP215.
source: Thus, Kip2 acted like a nucleation factor in analogy to XMAP215 (Wieczorek et al., 2015).
evidence: Inferred from experimental data and comparison to XMAP215

claim: 40 nM Kip2 decreased the rate of dissociation of GMPCPP-tubulin subunits from GMPCPP microtubules (koff) approximately threefold.
source: Our observation that the catastrophe frequency decreased 10-fold might be explained by our finding that 40 nM Kip2 decreased the rate of dissociation of GMPCPP-tubulin subunits from GMPCPP microtubules (koff) approximately threefold (Figure 1—figure supplement 3B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in figures

claim: A decrease in koff is expected to stabilize the GTP cap and therefore inhibit catastrophe.
source: If GMPCPP-tubulin acts as an analog for guanosine-5'-triphosphate (GTP)-tubulin (Hyman et al., 1992), then a decrease in koff is expected to stabilize the GTP cap and therefore inhibit catastrophe (Bowne-Anderson et al., 2013; Coombes et al., 2103; Margolin et al., 2011).
evidence: Inferred from established knowledge and cited literature

claim: The increase in kon and the decrease in koff likely account for most of the decrease in the catastrophe frequency.
source: Thus, the increase in kon and the decrease in koff likely account for most of the decrease in the catastrophe frequency.
evidence: Inferred from experimental data and theoretical considerations

claim: Single Kip2-eGFP molecules associated with GMPCPP-stabilized porcine microtubules along the lattice and walked processively toward the plus end of the microtubule in 1 mM ATP.
source: Kymographs revealed that in 1 mM ATP, single Kip2-eGFP molecules associated with GMPCPP-stabilized porcine microtubules along the lattice and walked processively toward the plus end of the microtubule (Figure 2B, Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in figures

claim: The velocity of Kip2-eGFP on GMPCPP-stabilized microtubules was 5.0 ± 0.9 μm/min at 28°C.
source: The velocity was 5.0 ± 0.9 μm/min at 28°C (mean ± standard deviation [SD], n = 674 traces).
evidence: Supported by experimental data

claim: The average run distance of Kip2-eGFP before dissociating was 4.1 ± 0.3 μm.
source: The average run distance before dissociating was 4.1 ± 0.3 μm (mean ± SE, n = 217, Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in figures

claim: Roberts et al. (2014) observed a similar velocity for Kip2, though the run distance was shorter (1.2 μm).
source: A similar velocity was observed by Roberts et al. (2014), though the run distance was shorter (1.2 μm).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior published work

claim: At the plus end, Kip2-GFP resided for 30 ± 26 s before dissociating.
source: At the plus end, Kip2-GFP resided for 30 ± 26 s before dissociating (mean ± SD, n = 40, Figure 2D, Figure 2—figure supplement 1C), leading to an accumulation of up to 12 Kip2-eGFP molecules at the plus-end, based on the fluorescence intensity (Figure 2B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in figures

claim: Up to 12 Kip2-eGFP molecules accumulated at the plus-end, based on fluorescence intensity.
source: At the plus end, Kip2-GFP resided for 30 ± 26 s before dissociating (mean ± SD, n = 40, Figure 2D, Figure 2—figure supplement 1C), leading to an accumulation of up to 12 Kip2-eGFP molecules at the plus-end, based on the fluorescence intensity (Figure 2B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in figures

claim: When ATP was replaced by AMP-PNP, Kip2-eGFP tightly bound to the lattice and did not translocate.
source: When the ATP was replaced by the non-hydrolyzable analog AMP-PNP, Kip2-eGFP tightly bound to the lattice and did not translocate (Figure 2C).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in figures

claim: Kip2-eGFP moved slower on dynamic microtubules (2.1 ± 0.89 μm/min) than on GMPCPP-stabilized microtubules.
source: Kip2-eGFP moved slower on dynamic microtubules (2.1 ± 0.89 μm/min), but this velocity is still greater than the microtubule's growth speed, so Kip2-eGFP was able to catch up to the growing ends of dynamic microtubules and track them (Figure 2E).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in figures

claim: Kip2-eGFP was able to catch up to the growing ends of dynamic microtubules and track them.
source: Kip2-eGFP moved slower on dynamic microtubules (2.1 ± 0.89 μm/min), but this velocity is still greater than the microtubule's growth speed, so Kip2-eGFP was able to catch up to the growing ends of dynamic microtubules and track them (Figure 2E).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in figures

claim: Kip2's mechanism differs from that of XMAP215.
source: Based on these properties, we conclude that Kip2's mechanism differs from that of the well-studied microtubule polymerase XMAP215.
evidence: Inferred from comparison of experimental data with known properties of XMAP215

claim: XMAP215 targets ends by diffusion and capture.
source: XMAP215 targets ends by diffusion and capture (Brouhard et al. 2008; Widlund et al. 2011), increases both kon and koff (Brouhard et al., 2008) and has little effect on catastrophe (Zanic, et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior published work

claim: XMAP215 increases both kon and koff.
source: XMAP215 targets ends by diffusion and capture (Brouhard et al. 2008; Widlund et al. 2011), increases both kon and koff (Brouhard et al., 2008) and has little effect on catastrophe (Zanic, et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior published work

claim: XMAP215 has little effect on catastrophe.
source: XMAP215 targets ends by diffusion and capture (Brouhard et al. 2008; Widlund et al. 2011), increases both kon and koff (Brouhard et al., 2008) and has little effect on catastrophe (Zanic, et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior published work

claim: Kip2's ATPase activity is necessary for its activity.
source: Furthermore, Kip2's ATPase activity is necessary for its activity, while XMAP215 is not an ATPase.
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing ATP requirement

claim: XMAP215 is not an ATPase.
source: Furthermore, Kip2's ATPase activity is necessary for its activity, while XMAP215 is not an ATPase.
evidence: Draws from established knowledge about XMAP215

claim: Kip2 is a unique regulator of microtubule dynamics.
source: Thus, Kip2 is a unique regulator of microtubule dynamics.
evidence: Inferred from comparison with other known regulators

claim: Kip2 stalled at a force of 0.81 ± 0.04 pN.
source: Kip2 stalled at a force of 0.81 ± 0.04 pN (Figure 3A) and showed a nearly linear force-velocity relation with increased velocity as the assisting force was increased (Figure 3C).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in figures

claim: Kip2 showed a nearly linear force-velocity relation with increased velocity as the assisting force was increased.
source: Kip2 stalled at a force of 0.81 ± 0.04 pN (Figure 3A) and showed a nearly linear force-velocity relation with increased velocity as the assisting force was increased (Figure 3C).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in figures

claim: At high forces, Kip2 often slipped along the microtubule in the direction of the applied force without detaching.
source: At high forces, the motor often slipped along the microtubule in the direction of the applied force without detaching (Figure 3B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in figures

claim: The ability to switch from the slip state to the normal translocation mode is thought to increase processivity by linking together several shorter run lengths.
source: The ability to switch from the slip state to the normal translocation mode is thought to increase processivity by linking together several shorter run lengths (Jannasch et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior published work

claim: Kip2 is a processive, low-force motor with long run lengths and end residence times.
source: Thus, Kip2 is a processive, low-force motor with long run lengths and end residence times.
evidence: Supported by experimental data on force, run length, and end residence time

claim: The low force of Kip2 supports the idea that individual Kip2 motors transport small cargos such as dynein, Bik1, and other molecules rather than organelles.
source: The low force supports the idea that individual Kip2 motors transport small cargos such as dynein, Bik1, and other molecules (Roberts et al., 2014) rather than organelles, although it is possible that multiple Kip2s could cooperate to move larger cargos.
evidence: Inferred from experimental data on force and cited literature

claim: Multiple Kip2s could cooperate to move larger cargos.
source: The low force supports the idea that individual Kip2 motors transport small cargos such as dynein, Bik1, and other molecules (Roberts et al., 2014) rather than organelles, although it is possible that multiple Kip2s could cooperate to move larger cargos.
evidence: Speculative statement about possible mechanism

claim: The strong localization of Kip2 to the microtubule plus end accords with Kip2 being a regulator of microtubule dynamics.
source: The strong localization to the microtubule plus end accords with Kip2 being a regulator of microtubule dynamics.
evidence: Inferred from experimental data on localization and activity

claim: Without Kip2, microtubules grew at a length-independent, constant rate.
source: Without Kip2, microtubules grew at a length-independent, constant rate (black circles, p=0.06, Student's t-test on a linear fit to the raw data).
evidence: Supported by experimental data and statistical analysis

claim: At low (1–2 nM) and intermediate (5–10 nM) Kip2 concentrations, long microtubules grew faster than short microtubules.
source: By contrast, at low (1–2 nM) and intermediate (5–10 nM) Kip2 concentrations, long microtubules grew faster than short microtubules (p<0.0001).
evidence: Supported by experimental data and statistical analysis

claim: At high Kip2 concentrations (20–40 nM), microtubules grew at a constant, length-independent rate.
source: At high Kip2 concentrations (20–40 nM), microtubules again grew at a constant, length-independent rate (green circles, p=0.36); however, at these high Kip2 concentrations, we expect all the length dependence to be in the first few microns, which is not well resolved in these experiments (see green fitted line).
evidence: Supported by experimental data and statistical analysis

claim: Kip2 is a length-dependent microtubule polymerase.
source: Thus, Kip2 is a length-dependent microtubule polymerase.

claim: In the absence of Kip2, the catastrophe length of longer microtubules was less than that of shorter microtubules.
source: In the absence of Kip2, the catastrophe length of longer microtubules was less than that of shorter microtubules (Figure 4C, 0 nM Kip2, p<0.05, Welch's unpaired t-test).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in figures and statistical analysis

claim: In the absence of Kip2, the catastrophe frequency increased with length, as expected due to microtubule aging.
source: This reflects an increase in catastrophe frequency with length, as expected due to microtubule aging (Gardner et al., 2011).
evidence: Inferred from experimental data and cited literature

claim: At 5 nM Kip2, the catastrophe length of longer microtubules was greater than that of shorter microtubules.
source: By contrast, at 5 nM Kip2, the catastrophe length of longer microtubules was greater than that of shorter microtubules (Figure 4C, p<0.0001).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in figures and statistical analysis

claim: The inhibition of catastrophe by Kip2 is length-dependent.
source: This indicates that the inhibition of catastrophe is length-dependent.

claim: In the absence of Kip2, the catastrophe frequency increased with increasing microtubule length.
source: Hence, in the absence of Kip2, the catastrophe frequency increased with increasing microtubule length, whereas in the presence of Kip2, the catastrophe frequency decreased with increasing microtubule length.
evidence: Supported by experimental data

claim: In the presence of Kip2, the catastrophe frequency decreased with increasing microtubule length.
source: Hence, in the absence of Kip2, the catastrophe frequency increased with increasing microtubule length, whereas in the presence of Kip2, the catastrophe frequency decreased with increasing microtubule length.
evidence: Supported by experimental data

claim: Both the increase in microtubule growth rate and the prevention of catastrophe by Kip2 increase with increasing microtubule length.
source: Thus, both the increase in microtubule growth rate and the prevention of catastrophe by Kip2 increase with increasing microtubule length.
evidence: Supported by experimental data

claim: Budding yeast kinesin Kip2 promotes microtubule growth in vitro in a length-dependent manner.
source: Summarizing our results, we have found that budding yeast kinesin Kip2 promotes microtubule growth in vitro in a length-dependent manner.
evidence: Supported by experimental data

claim: The rate at which Kip2 translocates exceeds the speed of microtubule growth.
source: Because the rate at which Kip2 translocates exceeds the speed of microtubule growth, Kip2 catches up with the growing end of the microtubule (Figure 2E) where it promotes growth and inhibits catastrophe.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in figures

claim: Kip2 catches up with the growing end of the microtubule where it promotes growth and inhibits catastrophe.
source: Because the rate at which Kip2 translocates exceeds the speed of microtubule growth, Kip2 catches up with the growing end of the microtubule (Figure 2E) where it promotes growth and inhibits catastrophe.

claim: The length dependence of Kip2 leads to positive feedback: the longer the microtubule, the greater the number of motors that land on it, the higher the number of motors that can reach the plus end, and the higher the growth rate and lower the catastrophe frequency.
source: As a consequence, this length dependence leads to positive feedback: the longer the microtubule, the greater the number of motors that land on it (the microtubule acts as an antenna), the higher the number of motors that can reach the plus end, and the higher the growth rate and lower the catastrophe frequency.
evidence: Inferred from experimental data on length-dependent activity

claim: The microtubule acts as an antenna for Kip2.
source: As a consequence, this length dependence leads to positive feedback: the longer the microtubule, the greater the number of motors that land on it (the microtubule acts as an antenna), the higher the number of motors that can reach the plus end, and the higher the growth rate and lower the catastrophe frequency.
evidence: Inferred from experimental data on length-dependent activity

claim: Once a microtubule is long enough, it will effectively 'escape' catastrophe and keep growing almost indefinitely.
source: Hence, we expect that once a microtubule is long enough, it will effectively "escape" catastrophe and keep growing almost indefinitely, switching from a catastrophe length of only a few microns in the absence of Kip2 to a length ≥ 40 μm at high Kip2 concentrations (Figure 4C, Table 1).

claim: Kip2 'paves its own way'.
source: In this sense, Kip2 "paves its own way".

claim: By combining processivity with polymerase activity, Kip2 can perform an elementary 'computation' that switches short microtubules to long ones.
source: Thus, by combining processivity with polymerase activity, Kip2 can perform an elementary 'computation' that switches short microtubules to long ones.
evidence: Inferred from experimental data on length-dependent activity

claim: The computation performed by Kip2 differs from that performed by kinesin-8, a length-dependent depolymerase, which stabilizes microtubule length through negative feedback.
source: This computation differs from that performed by kinesin-8, a length-dependent depolymerase, which stabilizes microtubule length through negative feedback (Gupta et al., 2006; Mayr et al., 2007; Stumpff et al., 2008; Su, et al., 2013;Widlund, et al., 2011 Varga et al., 2006; 2009).
evidence: Inferred from experimental data and cited literature

claim: Kinesin-8 is a length-dependent depolymerase that stabilizes microtubule length through negative feedback.
source: This computation differs from that performed by kinesin-8, a length-dependent depolymerase, which stabilizes microtubule length through negative feedback (Gupta et al., 2006; Mayr et al., 2007; Stumpff et al., 2008; Su, et al., 2013;Widlund, et al., 2011 Varga et al., 2006; 2009).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior published work

claim: The positive feedback mechanism may operate in vivo and account for the phenotype of Kip2 deletion.

claim: In vivo, the rate at which Kip2 translocates (6.6 μm/min) exceeds the rate of microtubule growth (2.3 μm/min).
source: First, in vivo the rate at which Kip2 translocates exceeds the rate of microtubule growth; the respective rates are 6.6 (Carvalho et al., 2004) and 2.3 μm/min (Caudron et al., 2008).

claim: The run length of Kip2 (≈4 μm) exceeds the length of cytoplasmic microtubules (≈2 μm).

claim: Bik1 may be required to increase Kip2's processivity in vivo.
